para: The field of logic has produced, over the past century and a half, an extraordinary profusion of formal systems. From Gentzen's sequent calculi for classical and intuitionistic logic, through Łukasiewicz's many-valued systems, Girard's linear logic, and the paraconsistent and paracomplete families developed by da Costa, Belnap, and their successors, each generation of logicians has extended, restricted, or reorganized the inferential resources of its predecessors. The result is a landscape of incomparable richness — and, as a consequence of that richness, of incomparable difficulty to navigate. Individual calculi are studied with great precision. Their relationships to one another are understood only locally, by pairwise comparison or by the occasional systematic survey of a particular family. The global structure of the space they jointly inhabit — the question of what kind of object the totality of logical calculi is, what shape it has, what its internal topology looks like — has never been the direct object of a mathematical investigation. The present chapter begins that investigation.
